title: K-H-L
hook: kahal, kehillah: an assembly, a community

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sh-K-N: the mishkan, the Shechinah, and shachen, the neighbor. Your line was presence is neighborly. On day three hundred sixty-eight, Moses gathered everyone after the golden calf; today, the root of that gathering.

There's a book in the Bible whose author doesn't give a name, just a title: Kohelet. It opens with a man looking hard at life and calling all of it vapor, breath, here and gone. English Bibles call the book Ecclesiastes, and the speaker the Preacher. But Kohelet comes from a root that means to gather a crowd: something like the Gatherer, or the one who speaks to the assembly. A book this lonely-sounding is named for a crowd.
screen: `A BOOK WITH A TITLE, NOT A NAME.` → `KOHELET: THE GATHERER.` → `NAMED FOR A CROWD.`

segments.voice: K-H-L. Kuf, hey, lamed. Kahal: an assembly, a congregation. Kehillah: a community. And the verb, to gather people together. First, the great gathering. Near the end of Deuteronomy, Moses gives an instruction for the festival of booths, once every seven years: read the teaching aloud to everyone. Look who's on the list: "Gather the people together, men, and women, and children, and thy stranger that is within thy gates." Not the leaders, not the scholars: the whole crowd, kids and newcomer included, so that, the verse says, they may hear and learn. The rabbis called this gathering hakhel: gather. Second, the community that lasts. For centuries, a Jewish town's organized community, with its synagogue, its burial society, its charity fund, its school, was called a kehillah. It's the people who show up for a wedding, a shiva house, a bris, a sick neighbor. Some congregations still use the word in their names. Third, the warning. In the sayings of the fathers, Hillel teaches: don't separate yourself from the community. Hillel's word there is a different one, tzibbur, but the point lands on kehillah. You can learn alone, and pray alone, but the tradition keeps pulling you back toward the room full of other people. Even Kohelet, with his big questions, takes his name from the crowd he spoke them to.
screen: `KAHAL: THE ASSEMBLY.` · `GATHER MEN, WOMEN, CHILDREN, STRANGER.` · `KEHILLAH: THE COMMUNITY THAT SHOWS UP.` · `DON'T SEPARATE YOURSELF.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE CROWD.`

segments.voice: Let your circles come to mind as rooms full of faces: family, friends, coworkers, a class, a street, a congregation, and notice one that hasn't gathered in a while. Picture them at one table, then add someone usually left off the list, the newcomer, the stranger within your gates. If you pray, you can hold that circle in your prayer.

segments.voice: K-H-L. Kuf, hey, lamed: the root of kahal, the assembly; kehillah, the community; hakhel, the great gathering; and Kohelet, the Gatherer. Today's word.
Your line: community. At the great gathering, the kids and the newcomer were on the list too. Till tomorrow.

howItsDone: Jewish communities are often called kehillot, and Jewish life gathers people for prayer, learning and the life cycle; some communities hold a hakhel gathering in the year after the sabbatical year, recalling Deuteronomy 31.

chat.says: Why does Judaism keep pushing people to show up together, instead of just believing privately?
options: The Torah gathers everyone, kids and strangers too, and Hillel says: don't separate yourself.
Because Jewish prayer only counts when it's said with a full congregation present.
Because the Torah reading was only for leaders, and everyone else just came to watch.

notes: Editor pass: replaced the fork and first myth, which repeated day 1403's Deuteronomy guest-list item; fork is now Hillel's 'don't separate yourself', myth items are Kohelet as a title and hakhel.
Kohelet glossed as 'the Gatherer' / 'the one who speaks to the assembly': standard explanation from K-H-L, but the exact sense is debated. Confirm phrasing.
Deuteronomy 31:10–12: 'at the end of every seven years ... in the feast of tabernacles' (31:10) supports 'once every seven years' at Sukkot; 31:12 quoted from KJV. Confirm.
The term hakhel for this gathering is from the root used in 31:12 and is the rabbinic name (Mishnah Sotah 7:8). Confirm.
Kehillah as the organized community of a Jewish town (with burial society, charity, school): stated generally without dates. 'Some congregations still use it in their names' is general usage.
Pirkei Avot 2:4 (2:5 in some editions): Hillel, al tifrosh min hatzibbur, paraphrased; the script notes the word there is tzibbur.
